GDQ6.brief: GDD is short for game design document, a text that describes what you plan to build. A one-page version is short enough that people really read it, and it lets a team review the idea before anyone spends time building it. In this quest you write one page about your arena encounter, which is the fight that happens in your arena.
checklist: Write one page for your arena encounter. Use these five headings: Goal, Player verbs, Beats, Fail state, Tuning knobs.
Under Goal, write one sentence that says what the player should feel or learn.
Under Beats, write 3 to 5 lines in the order they happen: enter, first contact, pressure, turn, exit. A beat is one step in how the fight goes.
Under Tuning knobs, list every number you might change, such as enemy count, spawn delay, cover count and health. Write the current value next to each one.
Add your screenshot from above from quest LDQ33. Share the document as a link that anyone can view.
GDQ6.done_when: Send a link to your one-page GDD with all five headings filled in.

GDQ7.brief: A critique is feedback from other people on your work. Other people see problems that you have stopped noticing, so asking for critique is one of the fastest ways to improve a level. An iteration log is a list where you write down what feedback you got and what you did with it. In this quest you ask for critique on your arena, change something because of it, and give a critique to another person.
checklist: Post your arena in the #showcase channel with the tag Critique-wanted. Include a screenshot from above, one screenshot at eye level, and a link to your GDD.
Ask one specific question in your post, for example 'Is the left flank too safe?'. Do not ask a general question such as 'thoughts?'.
Start an iteration log. For each entry, write the date, the feedback you received, what you changed, and what you did not change and why.
Make at least one change that is based on the feedback, and write it in your log.
Give one critique on the /critique post of another person. Name 1 thing that works, 1 specific issue, and 1 next step.
GDQ7.done_when: Send a link to your /critique thread, your iteration log, and the critique you gave.

LDQ36.brief: Readability means that a player can understand a space with one look: where the danger is, where to hide, and where to go. If the player cannot read the space, your design does not reach them. Color and light are your main tools for this. In this quest you choose a small color key, apply it to your arena, and test that it still works when the picture has no color.
checklist: Write a color key of 3 lines: one color for threats, one color for cover or things you can climb, and one color for objectives.
Make one Material Instance for each color and name them MI_Read_Threat, MI_Read_Cover and MI_Read_Objective. A Material Instance is a copy of a material with its own values. Apply them in L_Arena_01.
Change the value, which is the brightness, as well as the hue of each color. This way the key still works in grayscale, a picture with only shades of gray.
Light the exit and the main objective so that they are the brightest things the player sees from the entry.
Take a screenshot from your entry bookmark. Then convert it to grayscale and check that threats, cover and objectives still stand out.
LDQ36.done_when: Send your color key, and the entry screenshot both in color and in grayscale.

GDQ8.brief: A designer-tunable actor is a Blueprint whose important numbers can be changed in the Details panel, without opening its graph. When you set it up this way, other people can use and adjust your actor, and each copy in the level can have its own values. In this quest you turn fixed numbers into editable variables, add helpful names, tooltips and limits, and place two copies that behave differently.
checklist: Open BP_Enemy or BP_Lever. Turn three hard-coded numbers, which are numbers typed directly into the graph, into variables, for example MoveSpeed, WaitTime and Health.
For each variable, tick Instance Editable, which is the eye icon. Also give each one a Category and a Description, which is the text shown as its tooltip.
On the number variables, set a Slider Range and a Value Range. These limits stop people from typing a value such as 99999.
Give one Vector variable the option Show 3D Widget. This shows a handle in the viewport, so the target point can be dragged there.
Place two copies of the actor in the level and give them different values. Play in the editor (PIE) to see both behaviors, without opening the graph.
GDQ8.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Details panel that shows your category, your tooltips, and two instances with different values.

LDQ40.brief: A capstone is a larger quest that brings together what you learned in the quests before it. Here it is one finished encounter space, a place built for one fight, with its layout, enemies, metrics, design document, critique and readability all in place. In this quest you finish the space, bring your document up to date, improve the space after feedback, and record one full run.
checklist: Finish one encounter space. It needs an entry, an exit, cover built to your metrics, flanks, high ground with a cost, a NavMesh, and 3 or more enemies.
Apply your color key and your lighting from quest LDQ36.
Update the one-page GDD so that it matches what you built. Check the goal, the verbs, the beats, the fail state and the tuning knobs.
Post the space in the #showcase channel with the tag Critique-wanted, and ask one specific question.
Make at least one change that comes from the feedback. Take a screenshot before and after from the same bookmark, and write the change in your log.
Record a PIE clip of one full run from the entry to the exit.
LDQ40.done_when: Send a PIE clip, your marked map from above, the link to your GDD, and screenshots from before and after the change you made after critique, with the link to the critique thread. A mentor or two peers must approve your work.

GDQ9.brief: A Smart Object is a place in the level that tells AI characters what they can do there, for example a spot to take cover or a place to stand and wait. It lets you put activities into the world, and the AI finds them and uses them. In this quest you follow the Smart Objects quick start guide and then place one Smart Object in your arena.
checklist: Follow the Smart Objects quick start guide in a test level.
Place one Smart Object in your arena, for example a spot where an enemy takes cover or stands idle.
GDQ9.done_when: Send a PIE clip of an AI character using the Smart Object.

LDQ37.brief: In a stealth encounter the player tries to get past the enemies without being seen, so the level works in a different way from a fight. Cover must block what the enemies see, and patrols, the routes that enemies walk, must leave a path open. In this quest you copy your arena and change it into a stealth version.
checklist: Duplicate L_Arena_01 and name the copy L_Arena_Stealth.
Change the cover and the patrols so that the player can cross the arena without being seen.
Take a screenshot from above and mark the patrol routes and the safe path on it.
LDQ37.done_when: Send your marked screenshot from above, and a PIE clip of a crossing in which the player is not seen.

LDQ38.brief: A vertical arena has several floors at different heights, so the fight also moves up and down. Every stair, ledge and drop must fit how high your character can step and jump, and the AI needs a NavMesh, the map of where it can walk, that joins the floors. In this quest you graybox an arena with two or three floors, which means building it from simple blocks, and you check it against your numbers.
checklist: Graybox an arena with two or three levels of height. Use CubeGrid, a modeling tool in Unreal for building simple block shapes on a grid.
Check every change of height against your step metrics and jump metrics, the numbers that say how high your character can step and jump.
Press P to show the NavMesh. Make sure it connects the levels in the places where the AI should be able to follow the player.
LDQ38.done_when: Send a screenshot of the arena from the side, and a PIE clip of moving between the levels.

LDQ39.brief: Pacing is how the intensity of a game rises and falls over time. If every fight is equally hard, players get tired or bored, so designers plan peaks and quiet moments, called rest beats. An intensity curve is a simple line drawing of this plan. In this quest you draw such a curve for three encounters in a row and explain it.
checklist: Sketch an intensity curve for three encounters in a row. Include rest beats, the quiet moments, between them.
For each encounter, note what changes compared to the one before: the enemy count, the space, or the verb, which is the main action the player uses.
LDQ39.done_when: Send an image of your curve, and add 3 lines that explain each peak and each rest.

GDQ10.brief: A spawner is an actor that creates enemies while the game runs. A wave is a group of enemies that appears together, and the next wave starts after the current one is beaten. With a spawner you can change the size and timing of a fight by changing a few numbers. In this quest you build a wave spawner Blueprint with values that can be edited in the Details panel.
checklist: Build a Blueprint named BP_WaveSpawner. Give it three Instance Editable variables, which are variables you can change in the Details panel: the wave count, the enemies per wave, and the delay.
Make the spawner start the next wave when all enemies from the current wave are destroyed.
Place the spawn points where the player cannot see them.
GDQ10.done_when: Send a PIE clip that shows two waves, and a screenshot of the Details panel of the spawner.
